sec.title: IP considerations and copyright
sec.p: MNML LMNL expresses and exploits concepts that have been in the public domain in living memory. As long as we have had digital encoding, we have had digital text encoding. As long as we have had strings, we have had substrings (segments or ranges) and offsets. This work seeks not to define anything new but rather to codify a terminology abstracted from established prior art. Evidence for this claim includes not only LMNL (2002) but also the work on which it was based (XML, SGML, OTA COCOA etc etc).
This specification is copyright 2026 by Wendell Piez. Please do not quote from or use this work without attribution.

The works in this and related repositories are provided with license terms (in place), generally as free as possibly given their own dependencies. Please assume licenses in keeping with a Creative Commons BY-SA license, providing credits and similar terms going forward.

sec.title: Guidance for builders
sec.p: To whom is this specification useful or interesting? Broadly, specialists in applications of text encoding we call markup languages.

list-item.p: You may be interested in applications of markup in the humanities (viewed narrowly or broadly)
You may be a skilled technologist interested in developing capabilities of markup technologies
You may be interested in XProc, XML and XSLT
Your overlap problem demands a systematic and comprehensive solution

sec.p: You probably need to be in at least one of these categories to find the work here of interest.

An alternative implementation that supports data interchange using MNML LMNL encoding is a long-term goal not planned for at this time (2026). At the same time, it is hoped that this specification and related documents help to raise the chance that this happens.

sec.title: MNML and LMNL
sec.p: MNML (pronounced "minimal") is Minimally Annotated Markup in LMNL (pronounced "liminal"). LMNL is the Layered Markup and Annotation Language (Piez and Tennison 2002).

This document specifies MNML, designed as a formal subset of LMNL: all MNML documents are also LMNL documents. However, LMNL is not defined here. Because LMNL is taken on as a design constraint, inferences can be made about it inasmuch as features of MNML LMNL must also be true of LMNL at large. But while all MNML documents are also LMNL documents, the reverse is not the case. MNML LMNL follows all the rules of LMNL, and then adds additional constraints: extension by restriction.

Features of LMNL excluded from MNML are out of scope for this document. They include structured and annotated annotations, LMNL atoms, and potentially other features. MNML's restriction on LMNL annotations is discussed in a companion article.

As a specification, this document seeks to be abstract and notional, and thus to represent no particular point of view. Where first person pronounds occur, we can refer to users of LMNL, present and former, or people who talk about, or used to talk about LMNL or MNML LMNL.

sec.title: Scope of definitions
sec.p: As a form of LMNL, MNML LMNL is a data model. Along with this model we propose a syntax called MNML LMNL syntax. It is also related to the LMNL initiative in replicating, for the most part, the proposed "sawtooth" or "sabertooth" syntax associated with the LMNL proposal and used to illustrated LMNL examples.
As noted, LMNL and LMNL syntax are not defined or even fully described here.

An instance of the MNML (LMNL) data model is a MNML (LMNL) document; it can be produced in any way at all, but in specific, it is designed to represent properties of documents and their parts that are represented in and by the syntax.

A MNML syntax instance -- a string of text -- implies and defines an instance of the model -- an abstract data structure -- when parsed and rendered as such by a MNML processor. Accordingly, MNML as syntax ordinarily takes the form of a file on a file system or digital data storage device, or a string embedded or stored in and retrieved from a database or (non-LMNL) document structure. (For example, a MNML document might be created using a Save As Plain Text option in a word processor.)
Features of LMNL not supported in MNML LMNL include atoms, comments, and structured annotations.

The MNML model describes a MNML document in the abstract, with its constituent parts: together these offer a conceptual structure supporting information processing and retrieval. (It is analogous to an XML information model next to XML, or the conceptual "rows" and "columns" of CSV next to a CSV or TSV instance.) Along with these structures, a definitive mapping is described from this syntax into the model.

In addition to the MNML model as an abstraction, two other data formats are defined specifically for the Laminator implementation of MNML LMNL, in this repository: an XML-based tag sequence model called xMNML, and another XML-based range model, called LAYERS. These descriptions are not normative even for MNML LMNL (much less LMNL in general), but they are useful inasmuch as they describe its implementation in the Laminator.
LAYERS stands for Layered Assembly of Enumerated Range Sequences.
(We describe the ranges in a layer as enumerated because they cannot always be produced by any known rule, but only by reading the document. They are extensional rather than intensional.)
Each of these formats has a schema in draft given in the Laminator library:

list-item.p: xMNML RNC (RelaxNG compact syntax)

sec.title: Conformance
sec.p: MNML LMNL is defined as an abstract range model, enabling a text or text value, a string, to be addressed by means of its ranges, abstractly defined entities describing their text contents and amending or decorating the text with annotations. Conformance to these specifications requires an implementation that uses this model (or, internally, another model to exactly the same effect) to provide for rules-based processing of information so described -- a set of ranges over a text -- to create new information sets. These results may be LMNL range models, which can be written out and expressed as LMNL or XML syntax instances. They may also be encoded in plain text; JSON or other object notation; XML; or binary formats.

Because of this, LMNL or MNML LMNL conformance ("does the application use the model?") may sometimes be difficult to verify by formal means, even assuming specifications are perfectly clear and complete.

In contrast, conformance to MNML LMNL syntax -- i.e., the fitness of a given string for processing as MNML LMNL -- can be defined (as below), at least in part, by reference to the grammar used to describe this syntax (and in the Laminator, to configure its processing). An instance that does not parse unambiguously with this grammar can be stipulated to be out of bounds, and the parser will be able to tell us why.

Accordingly, while the syntax can be provided with unit tests offering coverage of its features (and some testing of this kind can be found in the Laminator code base), the larger question of whether a piece of software is "using LMNL" or even "MNML LMNL" must be determined at the interface between this software and its users, including other LMNL users, and not (or not only) by whether and how it resembles the Laminator (or any other implementation) in either its results or its operations -- even while systems should be returning the same results for the same operations. (Some XML-based and object-based systems, especially those that use offsets over strings to identify ranges, are already 'LMNL-like'.)

Note however that we do not yet (late 2026) seek to define either an API, or a query language, for LMNL or MNML LMNL. Both of these will require again addressing the conformance and testability questions.

sec.title: Relation to LMNL
sec.p: These specifications seek to describe LMNL while defining MNML LMNL processing to support LMNL, or more specifically the features of LMNL captured and codified in the MNML subset. Features of LMNL that are not implemented by MNML LMNL may also be described, but nothing said here should be taken as a normative statement regarding LMNL itself, whether applying to a feature that is in scope for MNML LMNL (such as overlapping ranges), or one that is not (such as structured and annotated annotations).

sec.title: Files, strings and documents
sec.p: The "base unit" for parsing (processing) MNML LMNL data is a UTF-8 string. In these specifications we describe operations over files, but an implementation does not have to work with files as such, to qualify as a MNML LMNL processor, as the same operations can be performed over strings maintained in any form, and irrespective of the particular input/output operations related to maintenance and persistence.

Since MNML LMNL has no inclusion mechanism defined in the model (applications may merge documents according to their own requirements), there is practical synonymy between file and instance. Document describes the same entity again, except regarded as an abstraction. A MNML document can be produced from any file whose content is a string using the prescribed syntax; such a string, stored as a file, is a MNML file and also -- when parsed -- is a MNML instance.

For purposes of this (preliminary) specification, such a string is defined as any UTF-8 character sequence that can be parsed unambiguously using the iXML grammar for LMNL syntax designated by Laminator, namely ../lib/xMNML/in/sawtooth-syntax/src/mnml-lmnl-explicit.ixml at the time of writing, and deliver XML results from an Invisible XML parse of the input with this grammar.

The rules enforced by this grammar are expected to correspond (never to conflict) with the rules of the syntax described here. If and where they are found to vary, conformance itself must be considered undefined until the issues in question are resolved and documents revised or updated accordingly.

The purpose of close alignment with the Laminator and its iXML implementation here is to center its grammar as the locus of control for the supported syntax, not to create a dependency on Laminator or iXML. If treating this grammar as normative poses any kind of problem with regard to system dependencies (in future), the specification can be externalized or abstracted from the grammar in question, or from iXML in general.
An alternative LMNL or even MNML LMNL implementation might opt for a different syntax altogether (or many of them), in addition to or instead of sawtooth syntax.

sec.title: Characters: Unicode normalization, whitespace, notation and naming
sec.p: A "string" and hence a value is defined as a UTF-8 character sequence without normalization, where each character is distinguishable by a position in the sequence in combination with a code point for the character (or other unambiguous representation). Other text encodings MAY be supported by processors able to transcode them definitively into UTF-8. Additionally, processors MAY use alternative encoding schemes, or none at all, as long as they are able to read and write UTF-8.

sec.title: Unicode normalization and string comparison
sec.p: When Unicode normalization of a UTF-8 string results in a detectably different UTF-8 string, they are not considered the same: strings are the same only if they are also the same at the codepoint level, i.e. when decomposed into characters, with no further adjustment or normalization.
Applications may normalize strings in performing their operations but these are considered document modifications like others.

In specifications and documentation, we may sometimes use regular expression notation for character classes (\n for new line, etc.), but this is a convenience and the notation has no special meaning for MNML LMNL, which defines no regular expression or other character-matching syntax.

sec.title: LF, but not CR
sec.p: Throughout these specifications, line feeds in inputs are assumed to have been normalized to Unix-conventional LF, i.e. no CR characters are given in the data. Ensure your CR or CR/LF have been converted to LF to avoid any issues.
This can be considered an exception to the 'no Unicode normalization' rule except that it is assumed always to occur or never to occur, not sometimes.
[TODO: test to see if iXML parse enforces this?]

sec.title: Whitespace
sec.p: In the MNML LMNL specifications, whitespace defined as in XML: \s+ where \s is LF|TAB|SPACE. All whitespace in the data (not in tags) is considered part of the data stream and not subject to normalization, improvement or correction.

sec.title: Names
sec.p: In order to help ensure alignment with XML systems, names are specified as in XML: \i\c* (in XPath regular expression syntax).
Currently this rule is expressed in the grammar used to parse the syntax, mainly because many things are simplified when names are known ahead of time to be easily convertible.

sec.title: MNML LMNL Syntax
sec.p: MNML LMNL is defined in two parts, which can be used together or separately. MNML LMNL Syntax takes after LMNL syntax, nicknamed 'sawteeth' (by John C) or 'saberteeth' (by Alex Cz), and may be referred to as such.

sec.title: Syntax Description
sec.p: MNML LMNL Syntax defines how a string of characters is to be rendered as a markup stream to a MNML application. For convenience, the markup stream resulting from a syntax parse can be described as an XML document. A MNML LMNL Syntax parser is NOT required to emit or expose such an XML structure, but what it does emit must be rich enough (no information loss) that such a document could be produced from its result using appropriate means (depending on its form).

Such an XML document representation of the LMNL markup stream or tag sequence is implicit in the Laminator iXML grammar for MNML LMNL syntax, but the iXML grammar should be considered as informative with respect to its design, not normative. (The iXML grammar in the implementation captures additional information for convenience in this implementation. If it is useful, we can codify this XML and provide a schema for it.)

Strings of characters, or documents, that do not conform to the grammar, are not considered to be MNML LMNL syntax instances, and must be reported as such. A conforming syntax parser MAY refuse to process such an instance, rejecting it with an exception, and it MUST have a processing mode that supports this behavior, stopping and reporting an exception (nominal error) for the first detected syntax violation in any nominated input. In other words, where inputs do not conform to the grammar, a conforming processor MUST make available a report of detected errors or ambiguities to a downstream processor, if it does not error out as just described.

In addition to matching the requirements of the grammar with respect to character sequencing (rendering useful distinctions between tagging and text content), a string must also conform to a few rules for regularity in tagging, which enable the straightforward and unambiguous construction, by automated means, of the corresponding information structure in an implementation. For example, every start tag is required to have a single (determinable) matching end tag.
To help specify these clearly, they are given at the end of the syntax description.

sec.title: iXML grammar
sec.p: See the file at ../lib/xMNML/in/sawtooth-syntax/src/mnml-lmnl-explicit.ixml.

An iXML grammar is given for MNML LMNL syntax in the Laminator processor. It defines an XML target format for an Invisible XML parse of MNML LMNL Sawteeth instances, producing an XML format suitable for futher processing.
(For comparison, older iXML grammars may also be available, but none should be considered definitive of anything.)

If any conflicts are found between that document and statements made here, both interpretations must be considered in question until adequate reconciliation has been made. Commit dates for relevant files MAY be taken into consideration if there are discrepancies between this description, and the implementation offered. An implementation must always determine the "right thing" in any case.

sec.title: Escape syntax
sec.p: Three characters, reserved to support tagging in LMNL syntax, are not to be used otherwise in text streams: the two open bracket characters [ and {, and the reverse solidus \.

Sawtooth syntax uses the open brackets [ and { as its open tag delimiters (or 'start tag delimiters'). The close brackets ] and } are the corresponding close tag (or 'end tag') delimiters. These characters are used to make tags.

Because these characters direct a parser to read tags, representing the characters themselves can be accommodated with an escaped sequence as a representation, using the \ character as the escape. So: \[ and \{ for [ and { respectively, and \\ for the reverse solidus itself (\).
Unlike XML, LMNL syntax does not support escape sequences for character references, parsed entities or marked escaped (CDATA) sections.

The close delimiters ] and } are not provided with an escaped form: they do not need it, and their use would complicate internal indexing. When they appear in content they can simply be used like any other character.

list-item.p: Escape "[" as \[ and "{" as \{. Escape "" as \\
Nothing else is to be escaped
Using \ followed by anything but the characters [ { or \ results in an error
Using [ or { to indicate anything but tagging results in an error

sec.title: Tagging
sec.p: Ranges are defined by the presence of corresponding start and end tags in the data, whose placement is taken to mark the start and end of the range. Tag correspondence is determined by matching the range name (generic identifier) and (if present) tag identifier.
Tagging a range named "foo":
Tagging a range named foo with an overlapping range named bar:
foo and bar with a new range, baz (overlapping foo but enclosed inside bar)
The same, except with an annotation, ZIP=AAA, added to the baz range:

A grammar can be used to distinguish tagging from text, permitting a LMNL processor to make deterministic inferences about the ranges being represented. To map into MNML, however, other regularities must be observable (rules must be followed). These include the suitability of names and values as well as the unambiguous matching of end tags to their corresponding start tags.

sec.title: Start and end tags
sec.p: Start tags (or "open tags") in LMNL begin with [ and end with }.
The open delimiter [ is followed immediately by a range name, optional annotations, and the close delimiter {. So: [start}.
End tags (or "close tags") are similar, except they open with { and end with ]. So, {start] is the end tag for a range named "start".

sec.title: Annotations
sec.p: An annotation looks like a small range given in a start tag, end tag or empty tag, except:

list-item.p: No tags (start, end or empty) may appear before the annotation end tag is give
An annotation end tag takes the form {], with no name required or permitted

Whitespace can appear between annotations, for legibility, and must precede a first annotation given; such whitespace is not considered part of the data set and may not be respected (considered in processing
The characters "[" "{" "" MUST be escaped, as elsewhere, and will result in errors if found outside such a sequence.

sec.p: Also note: annotations MAY be given on end tags as well as on start tags. End tag annotations are considered to appear in order after the start tag annotations (in their given order) for the same range.

sec.title: Order of annotations
sec.p: The order of annotations on a range will persist, unless deliberately altered, in processing. In other words, annotations on ranges are ordered, and preserve the order in which they are given in the syntax (unless altered specifically). Annotations may use the same names as other annotations on the same range. They maintain distinct identities even when homonymous or even synonymous (same name, same value).

To keep the model simple, however, the fact that an annotation is given on a start or an end tag is not considered to be information. A LMNL processor may freely rewrite a range's annotations to appear on either its start tag or end tag, or to split the annotations between them, provided their order is respected. So an annotation given on an end tag might be moved to a start tag in reserialized outputs.

sec.title: Annotation syntax
sec.p: The syntax permits annotations to be on end tags as well as on start tags.

Since the model does not retain where an annotation is given, with the result that a serialized LMNL document does not retain whether an annotatio is given on a range's start or end tag, and is apt to move.
In other words, these are the same in the model:
While this is not the same (the values of the annotations have changed):

sec.title: Tag matching
sec.p: Each end tag matches a single start tag appearing before it, and is matched by it. Empty tags are not matched (even with other tags of the same name), as they are taken to start and end in one place.

When interpreting the syntax into ranges, a range is taken to begin with its start tag and end with its end tag, without respect to any other tagging (for any other ranges). For this to occur, tags must be matched. The end tag matching a given start tag, and closing the range it opens, is the next end tag appearing after all intervening start tags with the same name (including the tag ID, if given), working forward, have been closed. If no such start tags intervene (the usual case), the end tag is the next end tag whose name matches.
The value of the foo range with the annotation [qux}AA{] is "BBBBBBBDDDDDDQQ".
The value of the foo range annotated [qux}CC{] is "DDDDDD"

sec.title: Tag ordering
sec.p: Tags appear in a given order in the syntax, but this order is not retained in the model, In the model, the order of ranges can be determined (partly) by their start locations, but among ranges starting in a given location, no tag order is prescribed. There are also scenarios, such as merging two LMNL documents into one by consolidating ranges, where a correct tag order is necessarily undefined in the general case.

Since rules can always be made for specific cases, this is not really a problem. Ranges start at given positions relative to the text, never relative to other ranges, their beginnings or endings, or to tags; placement of tags with whitespace is sufficient to maintain their relative positioning.
might come back as
but tag order will not change if content intervenes:
in this case the ranges overlap; tags are only reordered in cases of enclosure or contiguity.

As noted above, slippage can also occur in annotation placement on between the start and end tags on a given range. Annotation order on a range should be respected, but all annotations can be given on a start tag or end tag, or split between them, without affecting the range.
may be normalized by a processor as

NB: this is because in the range model, ranges have annotations, and the order of annotations given in syntax is respected in the model; but no distinction is made between end tag annotations and start tag annotations as such.

sec.title: Rules for regularity
sec.p: Each start tag must correspond to exactly one end tag, which follows it in the character stream. This correspondence between start and end tags is the closest thing in LMNL to the XML rule that end tags must correspond to start tags (XML Recommendation 2.1): the difference is that end tags in MNML LMNL do not have to be the first end tag after the start tag they match.
As in XML, each end tag must similarly correspond to exactly one start tag, which precedes it.

By default, documents containing start and end tags with no matching tag should not be processed or discarded, instead producing exceptions and stopping. A processor MAY provide modes with exception handling for these problems, but they should be disabled by default, only enabled explicitly, and provided with defenses (such as runtime warnings).

Empty tags (for empty ranges) are not matched to corresponding tags, and empty ranges, even with the same name as other ranges marked by start and end tags in the same document, have no effect for purposes of matching.

A processor MAY report a warning when a tag ID (a name suffix with =) is given on an empty tag range name, as it has no effect in the general case. (It has no effect unless it conflicts with another ID, in which case it is an error.) Empty range tags never need tag IDs since they do not correspond with (match to) other tags but are "self-closing".

Tag IDs do not have to be distinct across the document, as they suffice, along with the other rules of tag matching, to provide for marking up arbitrary overlap. But overloading them with semantics (using "meaningful IDs") is not generally advisable, as they can be rewritten internally and are not guaranteed to persist when a document is rewritten. For tag IDs to be unique across the document is a requirement for "normal" MNML, as described below.

sec.title: MNML LMNL Normalization
sec.p: A set of constraints over tags defines a subset of MNML LMNL called normal:

list-item.p: No ranges in the document are congruent. Ranges that might otherwise be congruent have whitespace (at least) between their start and/or end tags, providing for one to enclose the other. Empty ranges appearing at the same position are considered congruent.

At any given position (offset) within the text contents, tags appearing there occur in this order: first end tags (closing ranges), then empty tags, then start tags (opening ranges). Alternatively this rule may be expressed as no end tags may appear after start or empty tags at the same offset, and no empty tags may appear after start tags at the same offset.
When ranges start together (at the same offset), longer ranges start first, their start tags preceding the start tags of the shorter ranges.
When ranges end together (at the same offset), longer ranges end last, their end tags following the end tags of the shorter ranges.
No annotations appear on end tags.
Within tags, annotations are orderly, with no line feeds between them and only single space delimiters.
No tag IDs are repeated; each is unique within tag IDs assigned in the document.

sec.p: Whether a MNML syntax instance is normal can be detected by static analysis.

Normal MNML LMNL is useful because it can be parsed, processed as a LMNL range model, and then reserialized (written again as tags and text) with a guarantee that outputs will resemble inputs with respect to tag ordering and labeling (tag ID assignments).

This is useful because these discrepancies can constitute noise when comparing serialized instances. Deltas between inputs and outputs, where inputs are normal MNML, should show only such changes as are introduced deliberately by the process generating the output.

For documents with no congruent ranges, normalization of MNML LMNL inputs in the Laminator can be accomplished by converting xMNML to the LAYERS model, then converting back. In the Laminator, any process generating results from the LAYERS model specifically will ordinarily produce normal MNML -- whereas the xMNML model is capable of retaining "original" tag ordering.
Normalization entails:

list-item.p: Adjusting tag ordering to prefer "clean enclosure" to "apparent overlap" of coterminous ranges
Altering or emending tag IDs
Moving annotations from end tags to corresponding start tags
Keeping whitespace consistent within tagging and between annotations

sec.p: But normalization cannot resolve range congruency without changing the contents of the document (for example, by adding disambiguating whitespace between adjacent tags).

When lossless bidirectional conversion -- round-tripping (i.e., minimal delta between input and output representations) -- is desired, yet congruency between ranges is an absolute requirement (that is, if it cannot be avoided in document modeling and representation), it is up to an application to stipulate which should be inside and which should be outside. For example, an application could declare that ranges called div0 should always enclose div1 ranges rather than the opposite (and indeed that a divN hierarchy should be cleanly represented in the tag sequence).
An easier course is to test for and prevent congruent ranges along with the other normalization constraints. Whitespace or any other content between tags will prevent those tags from being reordered.

Note finally that these guidelines do not prevent a MNML LMNL processor from retaining original tag order (even anomalous or not normal), whenever possible, in serializing MNML LMNL documents as text strings (text and markup).

sec.title: Naming
sec.p: As noted, names in MNML LMNL must follow the XML naming rules (XML Rec 2.3). This is primarily in order to achieve seamless mapping MNML LMNL data into XML-based systems in which names are constrained.
This rule is relaxed slightly for the name "tag ID" component, which by itself may start with any name character (\c), not only an XML name-start character (\i).
So a name matches \i\c*(=\c+)?, or alternatively (with groups to match captured substrings) (\i\c*)(=(\c+))? . A tag may not have an empty string as an ID component.

sec.title: Range (type) name or Generic Identifier (gi)
sec.p: A range name is given to a range to distinguish it from other ranges. Usually such distinctions are made not among individual ranges, but among range types. For example, a document may have many ranges named "paragraph".

sec.title: Anonymous ranges and annotations
sec.p: Anonymous ranges and annotations (that have no names assigned) are permitted in MNML LMNL, but not considered advisable, as a good use case for them has not emerged (at time of writing).
(QUESTION: is this a good idea or does the Principle of Least Surprise suggest we exclude them at least from MNML LMNL? They also do not serialize into XML nicely.)

sec.title: Range name 'tag ID' component
sec.p: A range name may have an ID component, called its "tag ID", to distinguish a range from others with the same generic identifier. The ID component is given as a suffix to the name prepended with an equal sign '='. This is ordinarily done only to disambiguate tagging in cases of arbitrary overlap, as ID components are not intended for any other useful purpose. Such an identifier MAY be preserved internally so it can be used again when a document is serialized (written out) again, after processing, for the convenience of users; but applications are also free to rewrite them if necessary or useful. When a truly persistent identifier is needed (in contrast) one can be provided as an annotation: do not use the tag ID for this purpose.

Ordinarily, it should never be necessary to assign such a tag ID to a range except to resolve cases of arbitrary overlap, where by default enclosure would be assumed, and we actually have overlap. See below on arbitrary overlap.
If a tag ID appears on a start or end tag indicates it is to be matched only with the corresponding (end or start) tag with the same combination of range (type) name (GI) and tag ID.
Two ranges named foo overlap, one with the tag ID fud:

Note that the ID component of a name is typically not used as an internal identifier and should not be overloaded for this purpose, but simply used as a name part. (It can be regarded as a first name given to disambiguate a surname among siblings.)
Annotation names are not distinguished with ID components: the character = is not permitted in annotation names, and results in an error.
For convenience in working with XML names, all names in LMNL syntax (not their ID parts) must follow the XML naming rules -- informally, names much match \i\c* in XPath regex syntax.
Normal MNML LMNL, every tag ID is unique among tag IDs in the same document instance.

sec.title: Homonymy and synonymy
sec.p: Two ranges are homonymous if they have the same type name (GI), irrespective of a tag ID. More loosely they are said to have the same type. LMNL as conventionally used will reflect XML practice in this, for example naming all paragraphs p or para(these being ranges in LMNL, not elements).

It must be kept in mind, however, that two ranges have the same type by virtue of being named the same, and nothing else - type assignment is nominal, and types need not be defined intensionally (for example, as sharing defined characteristics or properties) or tested in any way, but are merely accepted as assigned and defined extensionally. A type is what it is (a kind of string, presumably), and two ranges are the same type because their tags (range type names or generic identifiers) say they are.

If two ranges have the same name (irrespective of ID) and their annotations are the same with respect to their names and annotation order, the ranges can be described as synonymous - they 'say the same (thing)'. Ranges that are both synonymous and congruent (occupy the same regions in the frontier) are possible - this is described as collision, and it may be wise to design such that this does not occur (or is detected and inhibited by validation rules). One reason not to prohibit this is in case it actually reflects features or properties of interest; another is to simplify and smooth interchange with other markup notations (XML and others) by not prohibiting phenomena that result from their conversion.
sec.code: [div}[div}Neither enclosing, nor overlapping: congruent synonymous ranges{div]{div]
[div [type}chapter{]}[div [type}section{]}No longer synonymous but still confusing, because the ranges are congruent while the tagging is ambiguous: tag order does not define enclosure{div]{div]
sec.p: In this example, the section appears clearly enclosed by the chapter. The chapter (or: the div range of type chapter), not the section, has an annotation named no with value "3".
sec.code: [div [type}chapter{]} [div [type}section{]}Here the section is clearly inside the chapter, as the line break (whitespace) between tags clarifies range boundaries.{div]{div [no}3{]]

sec.title: Avoiding synonymy - range name overloading
sec.p: Ranges that are both synonymous and congruent can be especially problematic as they appear to be identical in all respects, but their identities are retained in the model (visible to application processing). Without a warrant from application logic, a processor is not free to collapse them or remove one in favor of the other. To avoid the confusion this can cause, annotations can be used to help distinguish ranges with the same type name (generic identifier), so ranges of the same nominal type are homonymous, but not synonymous. Alternatively range names can be overloaded, as was sometimes done in SGML. So not just div but div1, div2 etc. can make suitable range names, with the numeral indicating the nominal "depth" of the range, when interpolating a hierarchy by the relative enclosure. (And a div0/div1/div2 hierarchy can be rendered as a plain div/div/div hierarchy in an application.)

Since the model can "see" enclosure but not hierarchy (in the sense that it is registered and made salient), the names help clarify both range boundaries and the (nominally or provisionally) "intended" hierarchy in the overloaded names. At the same time, the information as given (in this case, the nesting level) is subject to testing and validation. Rather than a necessary reflection of the design of the document, such tagging -- or so it becomes possible to regard it -- becomes a claim made with respect to it.

Another way to put it is that since the (hierarchical) "model of the text" is not given by the schema or syntax, it becomes a significant and emergent property of the instance or set of instances being described. Careful assignment of type names, along with principled rules around using whitespace and normalization, will avoid many of the kinds of ambiguities and collisions that can cause bugs and unexpected outcomes.

sec.title: Colons in names
sec.p: Colons in names are like any other name character, but applications may appropriate them for use. For example, binding names to namespaces the way XML does can be a useful way of differentiating between range families (layers) explicitly in the tagging. But this is true of any permitted character: such application semantics are not part of MNML LMNL as such and are not expected to be portable across implementations (work the same), without prior coordination. In general, MNML LMNL processors are not expected to do anything special with colons or names containing colons.
In brief: there is nothing special about colons in names in MNML LMNL, but there might be in LMNL applications.

sec.title: Document frontier ('base layer')
sec.p: A "base layer" is available to any LMNL document irrespective of other ranges indicated by markup, consisting of the document text value itself. This is also called the "frontier". It does not appear as a range in the model, but inasmuch as layers (selections of ranges) can be built on other layers, all layers in the model are considered to reference the base layer.

When documents start with a start tag, and end with the end tag corresponding to the start tag, they have at least one range congruent with the base layer. It is not a requirement for MNML LMNL that there be a single (nominal) "document range", although this may be convenient.
Note that whitespace after the last end tag of a document is sufficient to make the frontier (the document base layer) different from the value of the range that was closed with that tag.

In LMNL, each annotation has its own frontier (base layer), namely its text content, but since MNLM LMNL annotations constitute name/value pairs (with no structure or markup), their frontiers are effectively the same as their values.

sec.title: Ranges, annotations and values
sec.p: Ranges have identity and are distinguishable from other ranges by:

list-item.p: The frontier (UTF string value) they are bound to
Relation to frontier (offset and extent) - i.e. the region occupied
Their names, annotations and the order of annotations
Where they came from - they exist because an upstream source warrants them

sec.p: Because they are distinguishable does not mean they are not 'the same' if an application says they are - it is possible for an application to build higher-order structures from ranges.

There are cases (described below) where ranges become difficult to distinguish, especially if their provenance (fourth item above) is not tracked; this will for example be the regular case when LMNL documents are synthesized from multiple streams. These difficulties are described below; in general, as they occur predictably depending on naming and tagging practices in the data, rules can be introduced to ensure regular and predictable results from controlled inputs.
Note that ranges are always defined in relation to the entire document, and independently of one another.

In MNML LMNL, "values" are always strings. Applications may cast strings into typed data or object structures to support features, but this is not part of MNML LMNL. No special provision is made for numeric data types, Booleans, dates and durations or any complex data at the syntax level, while applications (including validators) are free to constrain these strings appropriately.

The values of all ranges in LMNL are determined in reference to their base layer (the document frontier), which does not change even if ranges are reallocated from one layer to another. (In the Laminator, ranges can be in only one layer at a time.) A single document has only a single frontier, however many layers are used to manage its ranges. However ranges are defined (whether by markup or other means), they are implicitly anchored to their locations ('regions') within this string.
The value of a range corresponds to the value of the text appearing before its start and end tags, excluding any other tagging.
The value of an annotation corresponds with the value of the text appearing before the end-annotation delimiter {].
Note that two ranges that are not congruent can have equal values (their texts can be the same). These substrings should still be distinguishable as occupying different segments of the frontier.
Ranges that are congruent necessarily also have the same value - while the meaning of that value may not be the same on two different ranges, even congruent ones.

sec.title: Range values and the xMNML model (Laminator implementation)
sec.p: (move this section?)

In the LAYERS model, the frontier (base layer) is exposed in its simple form, but in the xMNML LMNL model, it is split across nominal text value elements, each one linking to the ranges thate enclose (cover) them.

This makes the xMNML model a virtual "database" to the MNML LMNL document. Given a range, finding all the text that belongs only to that range is easily acquired, by splicing together all the text value elements keyed to that range.
Spliced together, these xMNML text elements have the same value as the region (or text segment) of the frontier (or base layer) occupied by the range to which they belong.

Similarly, finding all the ranges covering or overlapping with the given range can be done without looking at the entire text, or all ranges, by locating text elements that are (or are not) assigned to the ranges in question.
The base layer is not kept in an xMNML document explicitly, being the collection of all the text value elements.

sec.title: Terminology of range relations
sec.p: One range can enclose another range if it starts before or with it and ends after or with it. An enclosed range, however, is not said to be "contained" by its enclosing range, inasmuch as there is no generally necessary hierarchy among arbitrary ranges, whose semantics may be entirely disjunct, in the general case. Are pages inside the chapter, or is the chapter inside the pages?
Two ranges that do not overlap are considered to be discrete.
A range precedes another range if it ends before, or with, the other's start, and follows another range if it starts after, or with, the other's end.

Two ranges are coterminous if any of their start or end positions occur together. A range that ends where another range starts is coterminous with it, but discrete. When one range starts together with another, they are coterminous, and one encloses the other (or congrues with it).

Note that these rules mean that the binding of tags to ranges happens irrespective of tag ordering at any given position of text. The start tags for two ranges that start together can come in either order: to a MNML LMNL processor, they start in the same position and are co-terminous in either case.

Coterminous ranges can be problematic in some situations, if tag ordering is considered significant. Preventing and resolving such problems (in view of intended range semantics) is not usually difficult (see above for normal MNML LMNL syntax.)

A MNML LMNL processor MAY optionally trace tag ordering internally, for use when possible or useful in offering either warnings (if tag re-ordering is considered noteworthy) or options to preserve tag ordering where possible. (The Laminator processing library does not currently do this, although it does preserve tag line numbers and offsets of tags in a LMNL syntax source document, which could be used similarly.)

Annotations are not considered to be contiguous with other annotations even when they are not separated with whitespace in the syntax. They are considered to be ordered with respect to their parent or home range, but MNML LMNL does not require retaining whitespace as given within tags in a source syntax instance, when processing or serializing.

Two ranges that start and end in the same place are considered congruent. Every range in a set of congruent ranges encloses each of the other ranges in the set, as enclosure is mutual among congruent ranges, as are overlap and discreteness among ranges that are overlapping or discrete. Note that an enclosing or enclosed range is not said to overlap the range that encloses it or is enclosed by it, even though the ranges are coterminous, but not discrete.

sec.title: Arbitrary overlap ('self-overlap')
sec.p: Arbitrary overlap describes when two ranges with the same type name overlap one another. (In a looser sense it describes any kind of overlap at all, while overlap between ranges of different types is ordinarily assumed not to be arbitrary.) In the literature on overlapping structures in markup, this condition is called "self-overlap"; an alternative term might be "sibling rivalry". An example of this is when ranges are marked for indexing, with no special distinctions made among the ranges so marked that would motivate distinctive type names. The most convenient way to do this is simply to mark the terms (tags are tags) and let the processor do the rest.

Arbitrary overlap might raise a question for the parser as to whether two ranges named the same are overlapping, or enclosing/enclosed. To address this ambiguity, the LMNL syntax parsing rule (implemented in tag matching) is "most recent start tag wins", i.e. we match going "bottom-up" were we closing hierarchies (which we are not). To provide for the case where a prior start tag should instead be matched -- before the most recent preceding name match -- tag IDs (captured and treated as range name qualifiers ) can be given. With the ID treated as a component (qualifier) of the name (in both start and end tags), tag matching rules then do the right thing to match them.

Apart from supporting arbitrary overlap, tag (name component) IDs are not actually needed in LMNL tagging, since the placement, extent, and names (even "type names" or "family names") of ranges is enough to distinguish them.
sec.code: [div=0}[div}Here the tag ID makes no practical difference since the ranges are congruent and synonymous in any case (a bad idea) {div=0]{div]

sec.title: Layers
sec.p: Because ranges can be congruent - more than one range can span across the same region in the base layer - there is no limit to how many ranges can be identified in a document. Additionally, ranges can be, in general, defined implicitly instead of provided "explicitly" in the usual way, i.e. as markup. They can also be determined (defined or observed) by the application of rules ("all words starting with s ") or their descriptions using standoff markup. A MNML LMNL application may accept range definitions from a variety of sources. In particular, until a model is instantiated internally, not all ranges must be defined by enumeration or 'extensionally' (as is the cast for markup), and there is no requirement or expectation that MNML instances be acquired only by parsing MNML syntax.

In other words, it is entirely up to an application what it thinks important ranges are, or how it determines their presence. The syntax is one convenient way to assert the presence of (MNML LMNL) ranges over text. It can also be useful to acquire other kinds of sources (describing range sets asserted over a frontier), as well as to unify such information acquired in different forms.

This openness makes the primary work of a MNML LMNL processor the management and marshalling of ranges, by family and by type, arbitrarily according to application logic. The layers feature of the MNML LMNL model is proposed to help make such processing tractable, so that it can be specified, planned and implemented.

At present, there is no normative way and no single recommended way to specify that ranges belong to layers, in the syntax. To the extent that this is a requirement (it usually is not), a naming convention can be applied to tags. For example, in a simple case, upper-case tag names could identify ranges for one layer, while lower-case names identify ranges for another.) Application logic can then be used to separate ranges out into layers.
This makes it easier to optimize processing internally for operations such as casting from LMNL into XML, where distinguishing ranges layers can be convenient.

sec.title: Layers and hierarchies
sec.p: A layer is an arbitrary set of ranges enumerated explicitly. A layer may be created either by parsing markup and allocating ranges into layers according to application logic, or dynamically inside a processor.

Overlapping ranges MAY be assigned to the same layer; in the case of arbitrary overlap, this may be normal. At the same time, when ranges assigned to layers align so as to make hierarchies, this is detectable, as noted below.

By default, the Laminator parses a MNML instance into a version in which all ranges are collected together in a single layer, including overlapping ranges. Ranges always reference the base layer (string contents) of the document, no matter what layer(s) they are assigned to.

Layers are an optional feature of LMNL in the sense that whatever a processor does internally, designers are always free to use the simplest possible arrangement - a single layer of ranges sitting over a single base layer. (In other words, you can design and deploy your own 'layer semantics' over unlayered ranges.)

Being able to discriminate between sets of ranges, by allocating them into separate layers, is also a useful thing to be able to do. A single LMNL instance may have an indefinite number of layers; these do not need to be expressed directly (or even indirectly) in document the syntax, but may be implicit or introduced dynamically or interactively. The layers in a LMNL document are not intrinsic to it. Instead, they need to be considered as useful to applications in both maintaining and interfacing with families of ranges, whose categories (and indeed, whose entire 'life cycle') will depend on the applications in view, which are free to use range annotations and naming as semantic indicators in syntax.
Internally, Laminator maintains a LAYERS model for handling and working with layers.

sec.title: Overlap and layers
sec.p: Because MNML LMNL makes it possible to allocate ranges to layers, they can be kept and treated separately (in 'families') even if overlapping with respect to the document. That is, the layers collectively can contain overlapping ranges, without any of the ranges overlapping any others in the same layer.
Thus we can have a "pages" layer that overlaps a "structural" layer, with each of their range sets discrete, and each one a discrete hierarchy.

(Note this is different from keeping them in the same layer and detecting the layer has multiple hierarchies, as noted below.) Any given pair of ranges in the same layer will be one (and only one) of the following:

list-item.p: congruent,
or enclosing/enclosed ('nesting'),
or overlapping,
or discrete

sec.p: Ranges allocated to separate layers in a LMNL document do not have these relations, although layers can always be merged, in which case they do.

Thus these relations are undefined for ranges in separate layers, except when explicitly regarded together (as it were in a layer), and although their precedence (which one starts first) is clear in any case. Since the relations are scoped to the layer, to say two ranges overlap (or do not) implicitly asserts they are in the same layer, or can be assumed to be so.
In a MNML document parsed with no further processing to allocate ranges to layers, all ranges are always in the same layer.
div0 encloses div1:
div0 overlaps div1:
They are discrete:
They are congruent:
or (no difference in the range model):

sec.title: Overlap and values
sec.p: This classification (congruent/nested/overlapping/discrete) align with to whether there is complete, or partial, or no concurrence in the values of the ranges, considered as substrings of the document's value, or (equivalently) references to its base layer -- that is, not only by their text sequence but also their placement within the document.

Simply, the values of two congruent ranges are the same; the value of an enclosed range can be found as a substring in an enclosing range's value; two overlapping ranges will have some value (a substring of each) in common (within the base layer); and two discrete ranges will not claim any substrings in common from the base layer -- even if their values are the same, regarded as strings.
sec.code: [line}[phr}Of man's First Disobedience,{phr] [phr}and the Fruit{line] [line}Whose Mortal Taste brought Death into the World,{phr]{line]
sec.p: The substring "and the Fruit" appears within the values of both the first line (line range), and the second phrase (phr range). Both ranges can be said to occupy this region of the frontier.
Here, two different echo ranges have the same value, but are discrete, occupying different regions (substrings or segments) in the frontier or base layer:
Congruent ranges with the same type name are "colliding" or "in collision". Even when ranges collide, processors must respect range identity and persistence in naming, values and annotations.

sec.title: Layers and Ordered Hierarchies of Content Objects (OHCO)
sec.p: To be well nested is a property of a set of ranges and accordingly of a layer. It means that no ranges in the layer overlap any others in the same layer. Such a set of ranges can be straightforwardly cast into a hierarchical structure with no adjustment of range boundaries or splitting, reallocation or hiding of ranges or range markers. It is said to be an "OHCO" layer, in reference to the "OHCO" model of Renear, Mylonas and Durand (1993).

sec.title: Multiple Concurrent Hierarchies (MCH)
sec.p: An "MCH" layer is a set of ranges that does not qualify as an OHCO - some ranges within the set are found to overlap others. However, of the cases of overlap, none of the ranges overlap any others with the same name - i.e., no ranges exhibit self-overlap or sibling rivalry.

For example, a set of div ranges may overlap a set of page ranges, but none of the page ranges overlap other pages, and none of the divs overlap other divs. (Pages appear in sequence, whereas divs are cleanly nested.) This is called "MCH" because the structure represents multiple concurrent hierarchies.
Where ranges show arbitrary overlap - where there are ranges that overlap other ranges with the same name (and therefore presumed to represent the same type) - we have neither OHCO nor MCH.

These categories make casting into hierarchies easier to support and manage, since they can be detected early and acted on whenever appropriate. As secondary properties they are also subject to testing and updating -- since applications are liable to make changes that invalidate them, they must be kept in order internally.

sec.title: Validation
sec.p: LMNL semantics, like all semantics, are made in part by making a selection from available alternatives, which selection is not foreordained or predetermined, but which are constrained by those alternatives in ways that can make such selection meaningful. Those alternatives are stipulated by the applicable set of rules.
For example, the MNML tagging rules stipulate that a document that fails to parse using the grammar, is out of bounds: its ranges are not rendered and cannot be checked.
Once syntax rules are followed, however, ranges can be rendered, and become visible to processors, making them subject to new sets of constraints at higher levels.
XML provides a model of this architecture, and MNML LMNL is analogous, allowing for differences such as the lack of a formal schema language that accounts for overlap.

The fact that such a schema language is yet to come (at time of writing) does not mean that we cannot validate MCH - we only need to define it in terms we can test. The Laminator LAYERS model provides a way to do this, as might (similarly) any implementation of LMNL layers, where distinctions between sets of ranges can be made.
We can broadly distinguish between two layers:

list-item.p: Syntax checking is analogous to XML well-formedness checking, providing assurances for processibility but not much more. This constitutes MNML LMNL Syntax Conformance. Requiring and checking for normal MNML (i.e. with tag ordering constrained for persistence) is a syntax-level requirement, but is optional and not always necessary or appropriate.

Checks on vocabulary, annotations, annotation usage, structure, overlap or lack thereof, hierarchy, MCH, and arbitrary (expression-based) assertions can and should be done using logic at an application layer, i.e. not necessarily at parse time.

sec.title: Application scenarios
sec.p: The Laminator offers an implementation platform both for processing documents rendered as range models, and also for maintaining such documents in the form of markup. Both parsing and serialization -- reading and writing sawtooth syntax -- are supported, for any MNML LMNL.

However, parsing is not the only way to create LMNL documents and serialization is not the only way they can be exposed for further work. They can be created by any programmatic means, and outputs can include LMNL tagging, XML markup or anything else (especially any other text-based format).

The Laminator uses XProc to organize and orchestrate this open-ended set of processes. One important feature XProc offers for this is in its composability: the Laminator offers pipelines that can be combined as utilities in other pipelines. Specialized processing for particular tagging (application) profiles can be layered on top of the general capabilities given by the library.

Interestingly, this can be done in several different ways, using approaches with different strengths and weaknesses, making solutions to certain kinds of document (range) manipulation problems more or less tractable. Knowing the full range of these approaches is the best way of avoiding the unnecessary complexity that results from an operation done "the hard way" when an easy way is available.
It is not likely that a LMNL-based operation or Laminator pipeline will be ever be as good as generic XML and XSLT for structural transformations, as the model is not built for those.

At the same time, for some operations especially those relating to the management of overlapping ranges, and the structures in which they are found, MNML LMNL is highly convenient, and it is difficult to describe or limit the kinds of markup applications that might benefit from its capabilities:

list-item.p: Extraction of plain text cross-sections based on arbitrary criteria (markup or inferencing)
Traceable production of XML from 'sloppy' sources
Any kind of range-based processing
Modeling more complex and higher-order data structures
Modeling higher-level abstractions entailing discontinuity, range identity and networked range relations

sec.title: Methods and methodologies
sec.p: One of the most interesting features of the pipeline architecture is its openness to various complementary approaches to text and document processing, which have different strengths. The Laminator not only parses and writes LMNL and XML syntax, it also orchestrates XSLT (and XQuery), and it supports processing "raw text", that is, LMNL -- or XML -- tags-as-text. These approaches to document or range modification can be used together as well as separately.

LMNL has a broad range of potential applications that can be usefully distinguished, by scale and complexity; by the nature and form of the source data (whether sourced in XML, marked up automatically or by hand or ported in some other way); and by the required results. The differences between the methods may not be in their capabilities as much as in how easy they are to develop, apply and reuse when needed.
Indeed, the approaches listed here are only those prompted by experience with XProc-based pipelines. An XQuery-based, or a non-XML MNML LMNL engine, might offer others as well.

sec.title: METHOD: SYNTAX WRANGLING with MNML LMNL syntax - sawteeth
sec.p: MNML LMNL syntax has an iXML grammar, but parsing with a grammar is not the only conceivable way to work with this syntax and produce viable LMNL outputs. A MNML LMNL file is also a string and can be worked on using string processing.

Care must be taken to ensure syntax is still correct after such modifications -- no differently from modifying an XML file by hand, or as a string, an early parse after such a modification provides assurances that the information (however modified) remains intact and legible. Because LMNL constrains the order of annotations appearing on a range, it is even a little more amenable than XML to this approach.

sec.title: METHOD: manipulating xMNML (tagged text model)
sec.p: xMNML can be produced by parsing MNML syntax, or by conversion from XML with a deterministic mapping (treating XML as a notation representing a range model), or by other means, including programmatic ones.

An xMNML instance can also be serialized again using LMNL syntax, or it can be cast to XML using either of two methods, ripping and building. Ripping is quick-and-dirty but often effective. Building is more fault tolerant and more generalized.

Any document that can be "built" into XML can also be "ripped" into XML by subjecting it to certain modifications first, to resolve overlaps handled implicitly in "building". These modifications, or indeed any modifications, can be effected by changing the xMNML document within the XProc pipeline that handles reading and writing it.
Some operations over LMNL ranges and their values are easily accomplished using the xMNML model as a 'range retrieval' database. (As described briefly above.)
Refreshing xMNML - rules for rewriting IDs and text to an updated range set - this can be done by casting to LAYERS and back.
Use case: text segmenting by exporting selected ranges

sec.title: METHOD: manipulating LAYERS (range model)
sec.p: Merging and filtering ranges and range families are even easier to do over LAYERS than over xMNML.

It also presents the document's value (base layer) as a single string, making it useful for analysis of the data with no markup in play. For example, a LAYERS instance can be input to a process that interpolates and introduces new ranges reflecting analysis of the text in a new LAYERS document that can then be written to LMNL or XML.

Because the LAYERS model also permits storing, internally, structures that are not transparently expressible using the syntax -- such as sets of ranges that happen to form clean hierarchies (OHCO or MCH) -- they can also be useful for operations that can take advantage of these structures.

A generic XSLT can convert any LAYERS instance into the corresponding xMNML instance. Another one can create LAYERS from any xMNML. LAYERS instances can also be created directly from XML using a utility for that purpose.
Use cases: Analytic report of range usage; Range maps

sec.title: METHOD: SYNTAX WRANGLING WITH XML - 'slurping' and 'ripping'
sec.p: To 'slurp' MNML is to create xMNML or LAYERS (the internal formats used by the Laminator) directly from XML, without writing LMNL syntax first. Simple XSLTs can do this and it saves steps and cycles.

To 'rip' XML is to write xMNML tag sequence out in XML format. Every start range marker becomes an XML start tag, while end range markers become end tags etc. As long as annotation names are distinct on their ranges (since name collisions among sibling attributes is illegal in XML), and as long as tags happen to nest -- what we get from ripping is a text file that happens to be XML.

Necessary provisions can be carried out up front to suppress or rewrite where overlap prevents a clean mapping into XML. Such provisions can include introducing new (discontinous) 'wrapper' ranges to substite in for ranges that overlap, or marking their starts and ends with empties, which the ripper casts into XML empty elements for marking using a 'milestone' convention.

sec.title: Policy on AIs and code generation
sec.p: No generative AIs have been used for specifications, code, tests, examples or documentation in this project.
The "no AI assistance" rule may sometimes be relaxed for purposes considered (by a person) to be relatively innocuous, such as suggesting git commit messages or to support background research.

sec.title: Scaling (document size) and caching
sec.p: Parsing and tag-matching operations should scale O(n) i.e. linear to the size of inputs - do they?

list-item.p: Length of frontier
'Density' of ranges - how many ranges per character?
'Weight' of ranges - how heavily annotated?
Depth of nesting (enclosure) in tag matching
Where are the current bottlenecks? (including starting JVM)

sec.p: One notable property of MNML LMNL syntax is that violations of tag matching rules cannot be detected until the entire document has been ingested. This makes them a little more difficult to insulate from bad inputs than XML, which can report an error as soon as an end-tag matching rule fails.
LMNL tag matching rules are more like XML's ID/IDREF rules (which come with some schema languages), namely constraints on referentiality in general.
However, systems are also expected to be able to cache intermediate representations of documents and information sets to alleviate performance and maintenance issues.

sec.title: Metadata conventions and failsafes
sec.p: LMNL makes no special provision for document metadata as a constituent element of LMNL instances. In part this is because LMNL is conceived as a framework for the definition of application languages (markup languages), which may have such provisions (as do HTML, TEI and many other markup applications, but not XML as such).

This is also because (unlike XML) LMNL is not used strictly for structured data, but for loosely-structured or unstructured data; so it is less amenable than XML to including tagged structures in document contents within the document as such.
It is very convenient, that is, to "keep the metadata out of the frontier", and in LMNL, that means keeping metadata in annotations, the natural place for it.
Such annotations can include information regarding titles/creators/encoders/dates, identifiers and hashes of data contents, for robustness.
Unfortunately, MNML LMNL limits annotations to name-value pairs so they cannot be provided with further structure except implicitly (not in the LMNL model).
Accordingly, three approaches are recommended, if it is convenient to keep the metadata out of document contents:

list-item.p: Metadata must be on annotations, but they can annotate empty ranges when necessary or useful (subject to a receiving application's semantic interpretation)
Include links to structured metadata (external but local)
Accompany all LMNL with readme documents in their repositories, in a containing folder

sec.p: Suggestion: use TEI Headers for your Digital Humanities project metadata. It can even be stored out of line, or LMNL can be embedded in TEI.
